# Quality gates {#sec-quality}

Compilers and tools find whole classes of bugs before any user does, if you let them. Set
these gates up on day one; adding them to a grown codebase means fixing hundreds of findings
at once.

## Warnings are errors, for your code {#sec-warnings}

Turn on a strict warning set for your own targets:

```{.cmake filename="CMakeLists.txt"}
if(MSVC)
    target_compile_options(core PRIVATE /W4 /permissive-)
else()
    target_compile_options(core PRIVATE
        -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Wshadow -Wconversion)
endif()
```

Then make every warning an error, in the preset rather than in `CMakeLists.txt`, so you can
switch it off locally when you need to:

```{.json filename="CMakePresets.json (excerpt)"}
"cacheVariables": { "CMAKE_COMPILE_WARNING_AS_ERROR": true }
```

Apply the warnings to your code only. Headers of imported targets, such as Qt and your
vcpkg libraries, count as system headers, so their warnings stay out of your build.

::: {.callout-important}
## Strict for your code, quiet for everyone else's
Warnings as errors only work when every warning is yours to fix. Set the strict flags per
target, never globally through `add_compile_options()` or `CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS`, so third-party
code and the code Qt generates cannot break your build.
:::

::: {.more}
**Template:** `cmake/AppTargetDefaults.cmake`, which applies warnings, hardening and
sanitizers to every first-party target with one call
:::

## Qt's strict mode {#sec-strict-mode}

Qt keeps some APIs only for compatibility, although it considers them dangerous. One
definition switches them off for your code, and a second one adds the conversion that strict
mode leaves on:

```{.cmake filename="CMakeLists.txt"}
target_compile_definitions(core PRIVATE
    "QT_ENABLE_STRICT_MODE_UP_TO=QT_VERSION_CHECK(6,12,0)"
    QT_NO_CAST_FROM_ASCII
)
```

Set the version to the oldest Qt you support. It also removes everything deprecated up to
that version, and a newer Qt disables nothing more until you raise the number yourself. The
compiler then rejects code that compiles fine but misbehaves:

```cpp
QUrl url = path;                                     // a "#" in the file name starts a fragment
connect(&timer, &QTimer::timeout, [this] { tick(); }); // may run after this is destroyed
file.open(QIODevice::ReadOnly);                      // the failure goes unnoticed
QString title = name;                                // name is a char *: which encoding?
```

Instead, you write `QUrl::fromLocalFile(path)`, pass `this` as the context object of the
connection so it ends with `this`, check what `open()` returns, and say what the bytes are:
`QString::fromUtf8(name)`, or `u"Café"_s` and `"title"_L1` for literals.

::: {.more}
**Template:** `cmake/AppTargetDefaults.cmake`, which sets both for every first-party target

**Read more:** [QT_ENABLE_STRICT_MODE_UP_TO](https://doc.qt.io/qt-6/qtglobal.html#QT_ENABLE_STRICT_MODE_UP_TO)
:::

## Sanitizers {#sec-sanitizers}

Sanitizers make the compiler add checks to your program. When a check fails, the program
stops and points at the bug, instead of corrupting memory silently and crashing hours later.

| Sanitizer | Finds |
|---|---|
| AddressSanitizer (ASan) | use after free, buffer overflows, leaks (on Linux) |
| UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer (UBSan) | signed overflow, invalid casts, misaligned access |
| ThreadSanitizer (TSan) | data races between threads |

Give them their own preset and run the whole test suite under it regularly:

```{.json filename="CMakePresets.json (excerpt)"}
{
  "name": "asan",
  "inherits": "dev",
  "cacheVariables": {
    "CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS": "-fsanitize=address,undefined -fno-omit-frame-pointer"
  }
}
```

A report names the bug and the line:

```default
==4711==ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-use-after-free on address 0x602000001a30
READ of size 8 at 0x602000001a30 thread T0
    #0 0x104a1c3f8 in StrokeItem::updatePaintNode(...) StrokeItem.cpp:118
```

ThreadSanitizer needs a build of its own; it cannot be combined with ASan. MSVC supports
AddressSanitizer only.

::: {.more}
**Template:** `cmake --workflow --preset asan`

**Read more:** [AddressSanitizer](https://clang.llvm.org/docs/AddressSanitizer.html)
:::

## Hardening {#sec-hardening}

Sanitizers are too slow for releases. Hardening is their cheap cousin: checks that stay on
in the shipped app and turn silent memory corruption into a clean crash.

- Standard library assertions: `_GLIBCXX_ASSERTIONS` (libstdc++),
  `_LIBCPP_HARDENING_MODE=_LIBCPP_HARDENING_MODE_FAST` (libc++)
- Buffer checks: `_FORTIFY_SOURCE=3`
- Stack protection: `-fstack-protector-strong`
- On MSVC: `/sdl`, and `/guard:cf` for both the compiler and the linker

::: {.more}
**Template:** `cmake/AppTargetDefaults.cmake`

**Read more:** [OpenSSF compiler hardening guide](https://best.openssf.org/Compiler-Hardening-Guides/Compiler-Options-Hardening-Guide-for-C-and-C++.html)
:::

## Linters and formatters, one check {#sec-linters}

Each tool gets one configuration file in the repository. Your editor, the build and CI all
read the same file, so they never disagree.

| Tool | Checks | Configuration |
|---|---|---|
| clang-format | C++ formatting | `.clang-format` |
| clang-tidy | C++ bug patterns and modern idioms | `.clang-tidy` |
| qmllint | QML types, names and bindings (@sec-qml-tools) | `.qmllint.ini` |
| qmlformat | QML formatting | `.qmlformat.ini` |

Wrap the checks in one build target, so "is my code clean?" is a single command, locally
and in CI. A second target runs the formatters and fixes the files in place:

```sh
# clang-format, clang-tidy, qmllint and REUSE
cmake --build --preset dev --target check

# clang-format and qmlformat, fixing the files in place
cmake --build --preset dev --target format
```

::: {.more}
**Template:** `cmake/Checks.cmake`, which also checks licensing with REUSE (@sec-licenses)
:::

## The QML tools {#sec-qml-tools}

Qt ships its own tools for QML. Three belong in every project, and all three read the type
information that `qt_add_qml_module()` generates for each module (@sec-qml-modules).

[**qmllint**](https://doc.qt.io/qt-6/qtqml-tooling-qmllint.html) checks names, types and
bindings. Every QML module gets a `<target>_qmllint` build target, and `all_qmllint` runs
them all. A few useful categories are off by default; switch them on in `.qmllint.ini`, and
let any warning fail the check:

```{.ini filename=".qmllint.ini"}
[General]
MaxWarnings=0

[Warnings]
UnusedImports=warning
FunctionUsedBeforeDeclaration=warning
AttachedPropertyReuse=warning
```

Many warnings come with a fix that `qmllint --fix` applies; add `--dry-run` to see the
changes first. Each warning has its own page in the
[list of warnings](https://doc.qt.io/qt-6/qmllint-warnings-and-errors.html), with an example
and the fix.

[**qmlformat**](https://doc.qt.io/qt-6/qtqml-tooling-qmlformat.html) formats QML the way
clang-format formats C++, configured in `.qmlformat.ini`.

[**qmlls**](https://doc.qt.io/qt-6/qtqml-tooling-qmlls.html), the QML language server, brings
both into any editor that speaks the Language Server Protocol: completion, go to definition,
rename, formatting, and qmllint's warnings as you type. It needs your build folder, where the
generated type information lives. How it gets it depends on how your editor starts qmlls:
with `--build-dir build/dev`, or, if you cannot pass arguments, configure once with
`-DQT_QML_GENERATE_QMLLS_INI=ON` and the build writes a `.qmlls.ini` next to each QML module.
That is a setting for your machine, not for the project, so keep it out of `CMakeLists.txt`
and the file out of version control.

Two more tools are worth knowing by name. The
[QML script compiler](https://doc.qt.io/qt-6/qtqml-qml-script-compiler.html) runs during the
build and compiles typed bindings and functions to C++, one more reason to write typed QML
(@sec-typed-qml). [qmlprofiler](https://doc.qt.io/qt-6/qtqml-tooling-qmlprofiler.html)
records where a running app spends its time.

::: {.more}
**Template:** `.qmllint.ini` and `.qmlformat.ini`

**Read more:** [QML tooling](https://doc.qt.io/qt-6/qtqml-tooling.html)
:::
